ACCEPT. The even-bridge support-completion theorem, the equivalence of exchange terminality, and the exact cancellation of the interface correction are correct under the stated hypotheses. The iteration also preserves the original signed accounting without reusing donor tiles.The conclusion is the stated reduction: receiver charge decomposes into charges of completed pieces with no even bridge. It does not establish the unrestricted compensation inequality.I checked the recalled receiver identity as well. A useful auxiliary fact is that every actual matching block has connected intersection with each tile. This fact is true; I give its proof below, making that part of the ledger argument self-contained.1. Completion and perfect-matching factorizationWrite  $\widehat L,\widehat R$  for the completed pairs, distinguishing them from their endpoint sets  $L,R$ .Feasibility and degree preservationSince  $pq$  is a bridge, the only endpoint edge between  $L$  and  $R$  is  $pq$ .For an original selection  $t$  retained in  $T_L$ , there is an endpoint neighbor in  $L$ . It cannot also be adjacent to  $q$ , because both that neighbor and  $q$  were originally occupied. Thus the new selection  $q$  has exactly one occupied neighbor in  $\widehat L$ , namely  $p$ . Every retained original selection has at most its original occupied neighbors.For each  $v\in L$ , every original occupied neighbor is retained:Endpoint neighbors in  $L$  remain endpoints.Original selected neighbors are retained by the definition of  $T_L$ .The only possible endpoint neighbor outside  $L$  is  $q$ , and it is restored as a selection.Consequently,
$$d_{A_{\widehat L}}(v)=d_{A_H}(v)\qquad(v\in L).$$
The same argument applies to  $R$ . This proves feasibility and exact preservation of endpoint occupied degrees, including at board boundaries.Factorization holds for every perfect matchingLet  $F$  be any perfect matching of  $H$ . Then
$$|L|=2|F\cap E(L)|+|F\cap\delta(L)|.$$
Here  $\delta(L)=\{pq\}$ , and  $|L|$  is even. Therefore
$$pq\notin F.$$
Thus every perfect matching restricts to perfect matchings of the two sides. Conversely, the union of any perfect matching of  $L$  and any perfect matching of  $R$  is a perfect matching of  $H$ . Since an original perfect matching exists, both factors are nonempty.This proves the full bijection
$$\operatorname{PM}(H)\cong
\operatorname{PM}(L)\times\operatorname{PM}(R).$$
It also proves the required assertion about actual matching blocks. An internal edge of  $L$  occurs in a perfect matching of  $H$  exactly when it occurs in a perfect matching of  $L$ , and similarly for  $R$ . The bridge is disallowed, and all allowed-edge components remain unchanged inside their respective sides.2. Both directions of exchange terminality are validThe mixed-exchange reduction is sound, and it is the important step in the converse.A feasible mixed exchange has a feasible monochromatic subexchangeFix the perfect matching supporting an exchange. Let  $U_b,U_w$  be its black and white promoted vertices, and let  $F(U)$  denote their matching partners.The occupied set after the full exchange is
$$A\setminus\bigl(F(U_b)\cup F(U_w)\bigr).$$
Keeping only the black promotions gives occupied set
$$A\setminus F(U_b).$$
The restored vertices are precisely  $F(U_w)$ , which are black. They cannot be neighbors of any retained black promotion. Hence every retained black promotion has exactly the same occupied neighbors as it had after the feasible mixed exchange.Original selections remain feasible because the occupied set is still a subset of the original occupied set. The same reasoning applies to white promotions. Choosing a nonempty promotion color therefore gives a nonempty feasible monochromatic exchange.This does not impose any feasibility condition on omitted promotions after they revert to endpoint status.A completed-side exchange extends globallyChoose the side perfect matching supporting the exchange and extend it by any perfect matching of the other side.Every promoted vertex has the same occupied neighbors relevant to feasibility as in the completed pair. In particular, the opposite bridge endpoint remains occupied: it is a selected support in the completed side and an unchanged endpoint in the global configuration.All original selections outside the exchanged side can only lose occupied neighbors. Therefore the exchange is globally feasible.A global exchange yields a completed-side exchangePass to a nonempty black monochromatic exchange and orient the bridge so that  $p\in L$  is black and  $q\in R$  is white.If  $R$  contains a promoted vertex, restrict the exchange to its matching edges in  $R$ . A black exchange deletes only white endpoints, so  $p$  was not deleted. Furthermore, no black promotion is adjacent to the black support  $p$ . The new selection  $p$  itself has at most its one neighbor  $q$ , and retained original selections remain feasible. Thus the restriction is a nonempty feasible exchange in  $\widehat R$ .If  $R$  contains no promotion, matching factorization implies that no matching edge in  $R$  was exchanged. Hence no endpoint of  $R$  was deleted, and  $q$  remains occupied. The exchange on  $L$  is therefore feasible with  $q$  restored as its selected support.The other orientation and promotion color are symmetric. These arguments apply to whichever replacement perfect matching supported the original exchange, proving
$$H\text{ is exchange-terminal}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\widehat L\text{ and }\widehat R\text{ are exchange-terminal}.$$
As the setup specifies,  $H$  here means the isolated component pair.3. Tile anchoring gives exact receiver-charge additivityBoth geometric lemmas in §4 are correct.A disconnected nonempty endpoint subset of a  $2\times2$  tile must consist of its two diagonal corners. The intervening corners cannot be selected, because each would see both endpoints. They are therefore blank, leaving each diagonal endpoint at most two occupied neighbors outside the tile. This contradicts single terminality.Likewise, if a selected corner in an endpoint-bearing tile has no internal endpoint neighbor, the diagonal corner must be an endpoint. Each intervening corner is neither an endpoint nor a selection: a selected intervening corner would see both the given selection and the diagonal endpoint. Again the endpoint would have occupied degree at most two.Thus every receiver selection has its unique endpoint anchor inside its tile.A tile meeting both  $L$  and  $R$  contains a cross-side edge because its original endpoint intersection is connected. That edge must be  $pq$ . Therefore there is one shared receiver tile precisely when  $pq$  is intratile, and otherwise none.Let  $r_K$  be the receiver-tile count and  $s_K$  the number of selections counted in those receiver tiles. Put
$$\varepsilon=
\begin{cases}
1,&pq\text{ is intratile},\\
0,&pq\text{ is intertile}.
\end{cases}$$
Internal anchoring and the two restored supports give
$$r_{\widehat L}+r_{\widehat R}=r_H+\varepsilon,
\qquad
s_{\widehat L}+s_{\widehat R}=s_H+2\varepsilon.$$
For an intertile bridge, each new support lies outside its own completed receiver. For an intratile bridge, both new supports are counted in the shared receiver tile.Together with  $|L|+|R|=|H|$ , these equations prove
$$\rho(H)=\rho(\widehat L)+\rho(\widehat R).$$
The counts are exact, including their multiplicities.4. The excluded two-endpoint  $t=0$  bridge really is impossibleThe exclusion in §5 is valid and necessary for the stated correction table.Place the two endpoints in the top row of the shared tile. If  $t=0$ , both lower corners are blank. Each endpoint has one occupied neighbor inside the tile, namely the other endpoint. To reach occupied degree at least three, both its external neighbors must be occupied.In particular, the two vertices immediately above the endpoints are occupied and adjacent. Neither can be selected: it would see its endpoint below and the other occupied vertex above the tile. Both are therefore endpoints.These two endpoints and  $p,q$  form an endpoint four-cycle containing  $pq$ , contradicting the bridge hypothesis. If a required external vertex is absent at the board boundary, the degree requirement already fails.Also, the two remaining corners cannot both be selected, since each would then see its endpoint and the other selection. Hence a two-endpoint bridge tile necessarily has
$$t=1.$$
5. The same correction appears in  $X$  and raw  $B$  $J$  is additiveA full endpoint tile is an endpoint four-cycle. Its vertices cannot be separated by a bridge cut. It therefore remains entirely in one side.Completion only removes endpoints from consideration, so it cannot create a new full endpoint tile. Actual matching blocks are unchanged within the sides. Consequently,
$$J_H=J_{\widehat L}+J_{\widehat R}.$$
All nonshared tile contributions are unchangedInternal anchoring ensures that every native selection in a retained receiver tile stays with that receiver’s side. A restored support can belong to its completed receiver only in the shared tile.Thus the correction is confined to the shared tile.The correction to  $X$ For two endpoints, the even bridge joins different actual blocks. Its original contribution is
$$(2-1)\cdot1=1,$$
and each completed side has only one endpoint in the tile, so both new contributions vanish.For three endpoints, the tile endpoint graph is a path, its remaining corner cannot be selected, and hence  $t=0$ . The bridge contributes one cross-block edge. Let  $h\in\{0,1\}$  indicate whether the other path edge also joins different actual blocks. The contributions are:Shared-tile endpointsOriginal  $t$ Original  $X$ -contributionSum after completion $\chi$ Two $1$  $1$  $0$  $1$ Three $0$  $2(1+h)$  $h$  $2+h$ Four endpoints would put the bridge on a cycle. Therefore
$$X_H=X_{\widehat L}+X_{\widehat R}+\chi$$
with exactly the stated possibilities.Direct verification of the correction to  $B$ This can be checked directly from the raw definition, without invoking the receiver identity.Write
$$\Gamma=\sum_C\gamma_C,\qquad B=-\Gamma,$$
and let  $k_Q$  be the number of actual blocks meeting  $Q$ . The tile contribution to  $\Gamma$  is
$$k_Q(t_Q-2).$$
The endpoint terms  $\sum_C|C|/2=|P|/2$  add, and all nonshared tile terms are unchanged.Two endpoints. Originally the shared tile meets two blocks and has  $t=1$ , so its contribution to  $\Gamma_H$  is  $-2$ . After completion, each side meets one block, and the selected counts sum to  $3$ : one native selection and two restored supports. The combined contribution is
$$(t_{\widehat L}-2)+(t_{\widehat R}-2)=3-4=-1.$$
Thus
$$B_H-B_{\widehat L}-B_{\widehat R}=1.$$
Three endpoints. The shared tile originally meets  $2+h$  blocks. The singleton-side block is distinct from every block on the other side by matching factorization. Its original contribution to  $\Gamma_H$  is
$$-2(2+h).$$
Both completed sides have  $t=1$ , and their total block multiplicity is still  $2+h$ . Their combined contribution is
$$-(2+h).$$
Hence
$$B_H-B_{\widehat L}-B_{\widehat R}=2+h.$$
Therefore the cancellation is exact:
$$\boxed{
X_H-B_H
=
(X_{\widehat L}-B_{\widehat L})
+
(X_{\widehat R}-B_{\widehat R}).
}$$
This calculation respects the raw ledger: a tile’s selected count enters every block summand meeting that tile. It does not assign that count only to the selection’s anchor block. That distinction is particularly important when  $h=1$ .Neither exchange terminality nor  $\gamma_C\le0$  is needed for this common-correction calculation.6. The recalled receiver identity is valid for actual matching blocksThe following auxiliary lemma supplies a self-contained justification.Lemma: an actual matching block meets each tile in a connected setSuppose otherwise. The intersection must consist of diagonal corners  $a,c$  belonging to one block  $C$ , with neither intervening corner in  $C$ .A vertex with only one allowed neighbor has its incident matching edge in every perfect matching. Its neighbor can then have no other allowed edge either, so that entire allowed-edge component is  $K_2$ .Since  $C$  contains two same-color vertices  $a,c$ , it is not  $K_2$ . Each of  $a,c$  therefore has at least two allowed neighbors. Neither of its two intratile neighbors belongs to  $C$ , so both external neighbors of each diagonal corner belong to  $C$ , and their incident edges are allowed.By endpoint connectivity in the tile, at least one intervening corner  $b$  is an endpoint. Let its block be  $D\ne C$ . Its partner  $u$  in a fixed perfect matching must lie outside the tile, because both internal neighbors belong to  $C$ .Whichever external neighbor  $u$  is, elementary square-grid geometry supplies a unit square
$$a,b,u,v
\quad\text{or}\quad
c,b,u,v,$$
where  $v\in C$  and the edge  $av$ , or  $cv$ , is allowed.Choose a perfect matching containing that allowed edge in  $C$ , and retain a matching containing  $bu$  in  $D$ . These choices can be combined: every perfect matching restricts to perfect matchings of the actual blocks, and such block matchings can be united independently.Switching the two opposite matching edges in the unit square produces a perfect matching containing  $ab$ , or  $cb$ . That makes a cross-block edge allowed, contradicting  $C\ne D$ . This proves the lemma.Deriving the identityDirectly from the definitions,
$$\rho+B
=
\sum_Q(2-t_Q)(k_Q-1).$$
For a nonfull endpoint tile, its endpoint graph is a path or singleton. Connected block intersections imply
$$e_Q=k_Q-1.$$
For a full endpoint tile:If it meets one block,  $e_Q=0$ .If it meets multiple blocks, the connected block intersections partition the four-cycle into arcs, giving  $e_Q=k_Q$ .A full endpoint tile has  $t_Q=0$ . Thus, writing  $j_Q$  for its full-multiblock indicator,
$$(2-t_Q)(e_Q-k_Q+1)=2j_Q.$$
Summing yields
$$\boxed{\rho=X-2J-B.}$$
This also explains why “actual matching blocks” matters. Arbitrary block labels could exhibit a three-endpoint pattern  $C,D,C$ , which would invalidate the local count; actual matching blocks cannot.I recommend recording this lemma explicitly if the note is intended to establish the recalled identity without reference to the earlier ledger file.7. Iteration is valid, including several cuts in one tileRemaining cut parities are preservedRemoving an even bridge detaches an even number of endpoints. For any other bridge in the retained component, that operation subtracts an even number from one side of its cut. Its parity is unchanged.Therefore every scheduled even bridge remains even when it is cut, and every resulting piece has even cardinality.An original nonbridge lies on a cycle. No bridge belongs to that cycle, so deleting bridges preserves it. Hence no new bridges arise. The bridges remaining in a final piece are its surviving original odd bridges, and cut parity forces each of them into every perfect matching.Sequential completion is exactly the stated simultaneous completionEvery current selected support has a unique endpoint anchor. At a later split, it is retained precisely in the descendant containing that anchor.Induction therefore gives exactly
$$T_K=
\{t\in T:\text{its original endpoint anchor lies in }K\}
\;\cup\;
\{x\in P_H\setminus K:N(x)\cap K\ne\varnothing\}.$$
Each intermediate completion is feasible, so this proves compatibility of all final supports. It is not necessary to assume compatibility separately.An original endpoint may serve as a selected support in more than one distinct completed pair. The endpoint sets partition, and the signed identities account for the support multiplicities.The interface corrections telescopeLet  $\Chi$  be the sum of the corrections encountered in any sequential splitting order, with each correction computed using the current completed selections. Then
$$X_H=\sum_KX_{\widehat K}+\Chi,
\qquad
B_H=\sum_KB_{\widehat K}+\Chi,$$
and hence
$$X_H-B_H
=
\sum_K(X_{\widehat K}-B_{\widehat K}).$$
Together with  $J$ -additivity, this gives the repeated receiver identity.The instruction to use current selections is essential. For example, if both edges of a three-endpoint tile are deleted as even bridges, the first correction is  $3$ . The remaining two-endpoint tile then has one restored selection, so the next correction is  $1$ . Their total is  $4$ , matching the original tile’s  $X$ -contribution. Assigning correction  $3$  independently to both original bridges would overcount. The note uses the correct sequential procedure.8. The whole-board accounting uses every donor tile onceOriginal whole-component receiver tiles are disjoint: a tile meeting two endpoint components would contradict connectivity of its endpoint intersection.Every selected corner in a receiver tile belongs to that receiver’s separated pair by internal anchoring. An endpoint-free tile contains at most two selections, since three corners of a four-cycle would give one selected corner two occupied neighbors. Therefore  $D\ge0$ .Summing over the original tiling gives
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{mn}{2}-|T|-|M|
&=\sum_Q(2-t_Q)-\frac{|P|}{2}\\
&=D-\sum_H\rho(H)\\
&=D-\sum_K\rho(\widehat K).
\end{aligned}$$
Thus the signed condition
$$\sum_K\rho(\widehat K)\le D$$
is exactly equivalent to the coefficient-one bound for the original configuration. Requiring each completed charge to be nonpositive is a sufficient special case.The  $D$  here is necessarily the original  $D$ . Recomputing endpoint-free deficits separately for completed pairs would count physical tiles repeatedly. The proof does not do that.Likewise, additivity applies to the signed charge. Positive parts are not generally additive:
$$\left(\sum_K\rho(\widehat K)\right)_+
\ne
\sum_K\bigl(\rho(\widehat K)\bigr)_+$$
in general. Section 6 correctly retains the signed sum, allowing negative charges to offset positive charges once.Finally,
$$\rho(H)>0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\rho(\widehat K)>0
\quad\text{for at least one final piece }K.$$
That is the claimed localization. Completion changes endpoint-free deficits and the occupied configuration, so it does not identify a bridge-irreducible whole-board counterexample. The note states this limitation correctly.The two explicit failed-hypothesis coordinate examples are also valid. My acceptance concerns the general written mathematical reduction; I have not authenticated the separate verifier totals, externally named examples, or Lean artifacts. None is needed to establish the proof above.
